content: The 2019 Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services, as outlined in Web Annex I, provide detailed information on in vitro diagnostics (IVDs) for HIV diagnosis. The guidelines are published by the World Health Organization (WHO) and are available in an electronic version with ISBN 978-92-4-001180-9. HIV Testing Purposes and Assay Generations Manufacturers design HIV assays for specific purposes, including: Screening: Testing individuals without apparent signs or symptoms. Diagnosis: Testing symptomatic individuals to provide a definitive result. Aid for Diagnosis: Supplementary testing for symptomatic individuals. Staging: Determining the stage of infection. Monitoring: Assessing disease progression or response to treatment. Prognosis: Measuring factors linked to clinical outcomes, regardless of treatment. HIV serology assays have evolved through four generations: 1. First Generation: Utilizes crude viral lysate; detects IgG antibodies only. These assays have relatively low sensitivity and specificity. 2. Second Generation: Employs recombinant proteins and synthetic peptides; detects IgG antibodies with improved sensitivity and specificity. 3. Third Generation: Uses recombinant proteins conjugated to enzymes (antigen sandwich); detects both IgM and IgG antibodies, further enhancing sensitivity and specificity. 4. Fourth Generation: Combines recombinant proteins and monoclonal antibodies; detects IgM and IgG antibodies as well as HIV p24 antigen. These assays are particularly useful for identifying acute HIV infections and are often used for screening blood and tissue donations. However, the detection of HIV p24 antigen in many fourth-generation rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) has been shown to lack sufficient analytical and diagnostic sensitivity. Additionally, in late-stage HIV infection, waning immune responses may lead to decreased levels of HIV-1/2 antibodies, while rising levels of HIV antigen may be observed due to the disintegration of antigen/antibody complexes. Formats of HIV In Vitro Diagnostics HIV IVDs are available in various formats, each with specific operational characteristics: Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs): Include immunofiltration (vertical flow) and immunochromatographic (lateral flow) formats. These tests are quick, with results available in minutes, and can be used at all levels of healthcare, including community settings. Simple Assays: Include indirect solid-phase enzyme immunoassays (e.g., comb or bead assays) and agglutination tests. These require more time and are typically used in laboratory settings. Immunoassays (IAs): Include enzyme immunoassays (manual or automated) and chemiluminescence/electrochemiluminescence immunoassays. These are highly automated and suitable for high-throughput laboratory environments. Verification of HIV Testing Algorithms National regulatory authorities assess the performance, safety, and quality of HIV diagnostic products for use within their jurisdictions. WHO evaluates products for resource-limited settings through its prequalification process, ensuring that prequalified products meet quality, safety, and performance standards. Verification studies are conducted to confirm that a combination of products in a specific sequence can accurately diagnose HIV infection before widespread implementation. Verification studies involve three phases: 1. Preparation: Shortlisting candidate products (6–10) based on quality and performance criteria, such as WHO prequalification or stringent regulatory assessment. 2. Verification Panel: Establishing a panel of specimens (e.g., serum or plasma) to test candidate assays. Specimens should be collected and stored under validated conditions. 3. Study Execution: Conducting the study in designated settings (laboratory or point-of-use) and training study staff on standard operating procedures (SOPs). Criteria for Product Selection Products must meet minimum performance criteria: RDTs: Sensitivity ≥99%, specificity ≥98%. IAs: Sensitivity ≥100%, specificity ≥98%. Operational characteristics, such as hands-on processing time, time to result, and additional required items (e.g., specimen transfer devices, lancets), are also considered. Products should be stored according to the manufacturer’s instructions, and all necessary consumables must be available. Training and Implementation All test operators must be trained on relevant SOPs, including specimen handling, assay performance, and result interpretation. Training should be documented to ensure adherence to study protocols.
